claim: Tumor cells display features that are not found in healthy cells.
source: Tumor cells display features that are not found in healthy cells.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract introducing the topic of tumor biology.

claim: cherub is a long non-coding RNA that is critically required for the development of brain tumors in Drosophila.
source: Here we describe the long non-coding RNA cherub that is critically required for the development of brain tumors in Drosophila but is dispensable for normal development.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding of the study.

claim: cherub is dispensable for normal development.
source: Here we describe the long non-coding RNA cherub that is critically required for the development of brain tumors in Drosophila but is dispensable for normal development.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states cherub is dispensable for normal development.

claim: In mitotic Drosophila neural stem cells, cherub localizes to the cell periphery.
source: In mitotic Drosophila neural stem cells, cherub localizes to the cell periphery and segregates into the differentiating daughter cell.
evidence: The abstract describes the localization pattern of cherub in neural stem cells.

claim: cherub segregates into the differentiating daughter cell during mitosis.
source: In mitotic Drosophila neural stem cells, cherub localizes to the cell periphery and segregates into the differentiating daughter cell.
evidence: The abstract describes the segregation pattern of cherub during cell division.

claim: During tumorigenesis, de-differentiation of cherub-high cells leads to the formation of tumorigenic stem cells that accumulate abnormally high cherub levels.
source: During tumorigenesis, de-differentiation of cherub-high cells leads to the formation of tumorigenic stem cells that accumulate abnormally high cherub levels.
evidence: The abstract describes the mechanism of tumor formation involving cherub.

claim: cherub establishes a molecular link between the RNA-binding proteins Staufen and Syncrip.
source: We show that cherub establishes a molecular link between the RNA-binding proteins Staufen and Syncrip.
evidence: The abstract states this as a key finding about cherub's molecular function.

claim: Syncrip is part of the molecular machinery specifying temporal identity in neural stem cells.
source: As Syncrip is part of the molecular machinery specifying temporal identity in neural stem cells, we propose that tumor cells proliferate indefinitely, because cherub accumulation no longer allows them to complete their temporal neurogenesis program.
evidence: The abstract cites this as established knowledge about Syncrip's function.

claim: Tumor cells proliferate indefinitely because cherub accumulation no longer allows them to complete their temporal neurogenesis program.
source: As Syncrip is part of the molecular machinery specifying temporal identity in neural stem cells, we propose that tumor cells proliferate indefinitely, because cherub accumulation no longer allows them to complete their temporal neurogenesis program.
evidence: The abstract proposes this mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: Stem cells have the unique ability to both replicate themselves (self-renewal) and generate daughter cells with more restricted developmental potential.
source: They can do this because they have the unique ability to both replicate themselves (an ability termed self-renewal (Smith, 2006)) and to simultaneously generate other daughter cells with a more restricted developmental potential.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smith, 2006.

claim: Stem cells have been linked to tumor formation.
source: Besides their role in tissue homeostasis, stem cells have also been linked to tumor formation (Reya et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Reya et al., 2001.

claim: Tumor stem cells sustain tumor growth indefinitely.
source: They can turn into so-called tumor stem cells that sustain tumor growth indefinitely.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of tumor stem cells.

claim: Drosophila has emerged as a genetically tractable system to model tumors.
source: The fruit fly Drosophila has emerged as a genetically tractable system to model tumors in a developmental context and adult tissues (Gateff, 1978; Gonzalez, 2013) as well as to study naturally occurring tumors (Salomon and Jackson, 2008; Siudeja et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the developing CNS, neural stem cells called neuroblasts give rise to most neurons and glial cells of the adult fly brain.
source: In the developing CNS, neural stem cells, called neuroblasts (NBs) give rise to most neurons and glial cells of the adult fly brain (Truman and Bate, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Truman and Bate, 1988.

claim: Neuroblasts repeatedly divide into one self-renewing and one differentiating daughter cell.
source: For this, they repeatedly divide into one self-renewing and one differentiating daughter cell (Kang and Reichert, 2015; Neumüller et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kang and Reichert, 2015 and Neumüller et al., 2011.

claim: Disrupting asymmetric cell divisions can generate lethal, transplantable brain tumors.
source: Disrupting these asymmetric cell divisions can generate lethal, transplantable brain tumors (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Cabernard et al., 2010; Janssens and Lee, 2014; Knoblich, 2010; Lee et al., 2006; 2006c; 2006d).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The failure to divide asymmetrically has been linked to tumorigenesis in mammals, particularly in breast cancer.
source: Importantly, the failure to divide asymmetrically has also been linked to tumorigenesis in mammals, particularly in breast cancer (Cicalese et al., 2009), myeloid leukemia (Ito et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2007; Zimdahl et al., 2014) and gliomas (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies in mammals.

claim: Most Drosophila brain tumors originate from type II neuroblasts.
source: Most Drosophila brain tumors originate from the so-called type II neuroblasts (NBIIs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Type II neuroblasts divide asymmetrically into a larger cell that retains NB characteristics and a smaller intermediate neural progenitor.
source: NBIIs divide asymmetrically into a larger cell that retains NB characteristics and a smaller intermediate neural progenitor (INP).
evidence: This describes the division pattern of type II neuroblasts.

claim: Newly formed immature INPs go through a defined set of maturation steps to become transit-amplifying mature INPs.
source: Newly formed immature INPs (iINPs) go through a defined set of maturation steps to become transit-amplifying mature INPs (mINPs).
evidence: This describes the maturation process of INPs.

claim: A mature INP undergoes 3–6 divisions generating one mINP and one ganglion mother cell.
source: After this, a mINP undergoes 3–6 divisions generating one mINP and one ganglion mother cell (GMC) that in turn divides into two terminally differentiating neurons or glial cells (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008.

claim: Drosophila NBs exit proliferation once they complete a specified temporal program during which they generate different types of morphologically distinct progeny.
source: Similar to mammalian brain progenitors (Kohwi and Doe, 2013), Drosophila NBs exit proliferation once they complete a specified temporal program during which they generate different types of morphologically distinct progeny (Homem et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Maurange et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Correct temporal identity in NBs requires the RNA-binding proteins IGF-II mRNA-binding protein (Imp) and Syncrip (Syp).
source: It is thought that their correct temporal identity requires the RNA-binding proteins IGF-II mRNA-binding protein (Imp) and Syncrip (Syp).
evidence: This statement describes the molecular basis of temporal identity.

claim: During early larval stages, Imp levels are high and Syp levels are low.
source: During early larval stages, Imp levels are high and Syp levels are low.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of temporal identity factors.

claim: Over time, Imp expression gradually decreases while the amount of Syp increases.
source: Over time, Imp expression gradually decreases while the amount of Syp increases.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of Imp and Syp expression.

claim: Manipulating the opposing gradients of Imp and Syp changes the number and type of neurons made.
source: Manipulating these opposing gradients changes the number and type of neurons made (Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017.

claim: During each NBII division, a set of cell fate determinants is segregated into the INP.
source: During each NBII division, a set of cell fate determinants is segregated into the INP (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The Notch inhibitor Numb and the TRIM-NHL protein Brain tumor (Brat) are among the cell fate determinants segregated into INPs.
source: Among those are the Notch inhibitor Numb and the TRIM-NHL protein Brain tumor (Brat) (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Knoblich et al., 1995; Lee et al., 2006d; Spana et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of Numb or Brat leads to the generation of ectopic NB-like cells at the expense of differentiated brain cells.
source: Loss of these cell fate determinants (Arama et al., 2000; Bello et al., 2008; Betschinger et al., 2006; Gateff, 1978; Lee et al., 2006d; Wang et al., 2006) leads to the generation of ectopic NB-like cells at the expense of differentiated brain cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Formation of malignant brain tumors has been observed upon the depletion of downstream factors that normally maintain the INP fate.
source: Formation of malignant brain tumors has also been observed upon the depletion of downstream factors that normally maintain the INP fate (Eroglu et al., 2014; Janssens and Lee, 2014; Koe et al., 2014; Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When numb or brat are inactivated, the smaller NBII progeny fails to establish an INP fate.
source: When numb or brat are inactivated (Figure 1B), the smaller NBII progeny fails to establish an INP fate (Janssens et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2006d) and initially enters a long transient cell cycle arrest (Bowman et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006d).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: After a lag period, the smaller cell regrows to a NB-sized cell that has acquired tumor stem cell properties.
source: Only after this lag period, the smaller cell regrows to a NB-sized cell that has acquired tumor stem cell properties and that we therefore refer to as tumor neuroblast (tNB) (Bello et al., 2008; Betschinger et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006d).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NBIIs and ectopic tNBs are indistinguishable in terms of markers.
source: NBIIs and ectopic tNBs are indistinguishable in terms of markers.
evidence: This describes the similarity between normal and tumor neuroblasts.

claim: Both NBIIs and tNBs are characterized by the expression of self-renewal genes and lack differentiation markers.
source: Both cell populations are characterized by the expression of self-renewal genes and lack differentiation markers (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006d), but nevertheless behave differently.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006d.

claim: Shortly after entering pupal stages, NBs decrease their cell volumes successively with each NB division before they exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
source: Shortly after entering pupal stages, NBs decrease their cell volumes successively with each NB division before they exit the cell cycle and differentiate (Homem et al., 2014; Maurange et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Homem et al., 2014; Maurange et al., 2008.

claim: tNBs do not shrink during metamorphosis.
source: However, tNBs do not shrink during metamorphosis (Homem et al., 2014) and continue to proliferate even in the adult fly brain (Bello et al., 2006; Loop et al., 2004; Mukherjee et al., 2016; Narbonne-Reveau et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In contrast to wild-type brains, tumor brains can be serially transplanted into host flies for years.
source: Moreover, in contrast to wild-type brains, the resulting tumor brains can be serially transplanted into host flies for years (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Gateff, 1978), indicating the immortality of these tumors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Gateff, 1978.

claim: Mammalian homologues of numb have been shown to inhibit tumor growth.
source: Similarly, mammalian homologues of numb (Cicalese et al., 2009; Colaluca et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2010; Pece et al., 2004) and brat (Chen et al., 2014; Mukherjee et al., 2016) have been shown to inhibit tumor growth.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The human brat homologue TRIM3 is depleted in 24% of gliomas.
source: Furthermore, the human brat homologue TRIM3 is depleted in 24% of gliomas (Boulay et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014) and NUMB protein levels are markedly reduced in 55% of breast tumor cases (Pece et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Boulay et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014.

claim: NUMB protein levels are markedly reduced in 55% of breast tumor cases.
source: Furthermore, the human brat homologue TRIM3 is depleted in 24% of gliomas (Boulay et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014) and NUMB protein levels are markedly reduced in 55% of breast tumor cases (Pece et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pece et al., 2004.

claim: Progression towards a malignant state is an intrinsic process in brat tNBs that does not correlate with stepwise acquisition of DNA alterations.
source: Our results indicate that progression towards a malignant state is an intrinsic process in brat tNBs that does not correlate with stepwise acquisition of DNA alterations.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: Transcriptome profiling of larval NBs identified cherub as crucial for tumorigenesis.
source: Transcriptome profiling of larval NBs identified the previously uncharacterized long non-coding (lnc) RNA cherub as crucial for tumorigenesis, but largely dispensable for NB development.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: cherub is the first identified lncRNA to be asymmetrically segregated during mitosis into INPs.
source: Our data show that cherub is the first identified lncRNA to be asymmetrically segregated during mitosis into INPs, where the initial high cherub levels decrease with time.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: Upon the loss of brat, the smaller cherub-high cell reverts into an ectopic tNBs resulting in tumors with high cortical cherub.
source: Upon the loss of brat, the smaller cherub-high cell reverts into an ectopic tNBs resulting in tumors with high cortical cherub.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: cherub facilitates the binding between the RNA-binding protein Staufen and the late temporal identity factor Syp.
source: Molecularly, cherub facilitates the binding between the RNA-binding protein Staufen and the late temporal identity factor Syp and consequently tethers Syp to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: Depleting cherub in brat tNBs leads to the release of Syp from the cortex into the cytoplasm and represses tumor growth.
source: Depleting cherub in brat tNBs leads to the release of Syp from the cortex into the cytoplasm and represses tumor growth.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: Only brat RNAi tNBs formed tumors in host flies, whereas control NBs did not.
source: Similar to the transplantation of tissue fragments, only brat RNAi tNBs formed tumors in host flies, whereas control NBs did not (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing transplantation results.

claim: brat RNAi tNBs require intrinsic mechanisms that render them immortal.
source: Thus, brat RNAi tNBs require intrinsic mechanisms that render them immortal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transplantation experiments.

claim: In larval and adult stages, tumor brains, similar to control brains, showed two peaks corresponding to diploid (G0/1 phase) and tetraploid (G2/M phase) karyotypes.
source: In larval and adult stages, tumor brains, similar to control brains, showed two peaks corresponding to diploid (G0/1 phase) and tetraploid (G2/M phase) karyotypes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2A showing DNA content analysis.

claim: brat tumor cells showed an increase in tetraploid cells due to more dividing cells.
source: Although brat tumor cells showed an increase in tetraploid cells due to more dividing cells, we did not observe any aneuploid and polyploid karyotypes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: No aneuploid and polyploid karyotypes were observed in brat tumor cells.
source: Although brat tumor cells showed an increase in tetraploid cells due to more dividing cells, we did not observe any aneuploid and polyploid karyotypes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Tumor brains showed no recurrent amplifications or depletions of large chromosome regions.
source: Besides that, tumor brains showed no recurrent amplifications or depletions of large chromosome regions, although the detection of afore mentioned biological phenomena shows the ability to detect gross chromosomal aberrations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The few detected somatic point mutations did not overlap between the three tumor samples.
source: Similarly, the few detected somatic point mutations did not overlap between the three tumor samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Small insertions and deletions (InDels) were mainly restricted to introns or intergenic regions.
source: Small insertions and deletions (InDels) were mainly restricted to introns or intergenic regions (Figure 2E) and we did not identify regions (length 10000 bp) with such InDels common to all three tumor samples.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The data of primary bratk06028 tumors did not reveal recurrent DNA alterations among several tumors.
source: Our data of primary bratk06028 tumors did not reveal recurrent DNA alterations among several tumors nor could we detect abnormal karyotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: Malignant transformation is unlikely to be regulated through a stepwise acquisition of DNA mutations.
source: These results suggest that malignant transformation is unlikely to be regulated through a stepwise acquisition of DNA mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genomic analysis results.

claim: The cell-autonomous events leading to highly proliferative tNBs seem to be of transcriptional or post-transcriptional nature.
source: Thus, the cell-autonomous events leading to highly proliferative tNBs seem to be of transcriptional or post-transcriptional nature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of DNA alterations.

claim: 1372 genes were upregulated in tNBs compared to NBIIs (FDR 0.01, log2fold change ≥2).
source: In total, we found 1372 up- and 345 downregulated genes in tNBs compared to NBIIs (FDR 0.01, log2fold change ≤ −2 and ≥2, respectively) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 3C showing transcriptome analysis results.

claim: 345 genes were downregulated in tNBs compared to NBIIs (FDR 0.01, log2fold change ≤ −2).
source: In total, we found 1372 up- and 345 downregulated genes in tNBs compared to NBIIs (FDR 0.01, log2fold change ≤ −2 and ≥2, respectively) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 3C.

claim: CR43283 (cherub) was the upregulated gene most highly expressed in tNB.
source: The upregulated gene most highly expressed in tNB was CR43283 (Figure 3C), which encodes three alternatively spliced polyadenylated transcripts without any long open reading frames.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 3C.

claim: CR43283 encodes three alternatively spliced polyadenylated transcripts without any long open reading frames.
source: The upregulated gene most highly expressed in tNB was CR43283 (Figure 3C), which encodes three alternatively spliced polyadenylated transcripts without any long open reading frames.
evidence: This describes the structure of CR43283 transcripts.

claim: Peptides of short open reading frames found in CR43283 were not detected in the brat tumor proteome.
source: Peptides of short open reading frames found in CR43283 were not detected in the brat tumor proteome (Jüschke et al., 2013) (data not shown) and PhyloCSF analysis of CR43283 did not reveal any coding potential (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to a previous proteome study and Figure 3D.

claim: PhyloCSF analysis of CR43283 did not reveal any coding potential.
source: Peptides of short open reading frames found in CR43283 were not detected in the brat tumor proteome (Jüschke et al., 2013) (data not shown) and PhyloCSF analysis of CR43283 did not reveal any coding potential (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing PhyloCSF analysis.

claim: CR43283 likely acts as a lncRNA.
source: Thus, CR43283 likely acts as a lncRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of coding potential.

claim: cherub mutants were viable and fertile.
source: cherub mutants were viable and fertile, as numbers of eggs laid per female and of emerging adults were similar to control flies (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 4A,B showing viability and fertility data.

claim: cherub mutant flies showed normal behavior in a geotaxis assay.
source: Furthermore, cherub mutant flies showed normal behavior in a geotaxis assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 4C showing geotaxis assay results.

claim: NBII lineages lacking cherub appeared normal.
source: NBII lineages lacking cherub appeared normal (Figure 4D) and contained one large NBII expressing Deadpan (Dpn) but not Asense (Ase) surrounded by Dpn-Ase- immature and Dpn+Ase+ mature INPs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 4D, E, F showing NBII lineage analysis.

claim: In a cherub mutant background neither brat mutations nor brat RNAi resulted in the formation of large brain tumors.
source: Nevertheless, in a cherub mutant background neither brat mutations nor brat RNAi resulted in the formation of large brain tumors (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both tumor volumes and numbers of Dpn+ tNBs were strongly reduced in cherub mutant background.
source: Both, tumor volumes and numbers of Dpn+ tNBs were strongly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduction in tumor growth resulted in increased viability.
source: The reduction in tumor growth resulted in increased viability (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A genomic rescue construct was able to again increase the number of Dpn+ tNBs in cherub brat depleted brains.
source: A genomic rescue construct was able to again increase the number of Dpn+ tNBs in cherub brat depleted brains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: cherub is required for tNBs to form large brain tumors.
source: Thus, cherub is required for tNBs to form large brain tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: cherub was expressed in all central brain and ventral nerve cord NB lineages.
source: cherub was expressed in all central brain and ventral nerve cord NB lineages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In NBIIs, FISH probes against cherub stained two nuclear dots representing nascent transcripts.
source: In NBIIs, FISH probes against cherub stained two nuclear dots (Figure 6A) representing nascent transcripts (Levesque and Raj, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6A and a citation to Levesque and Raj, 2013.

claim: cherub was enriched at the cell cortex and was only weakly detected in the cytoplasm of NBIIs.
source: In addition, the lncRNA was enriched at the cell cortex and was only weakly detected in the cytoplasm (Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The highest levels of cherub were found in newborn INPs, where it was cytoplasmic.
source: The highest levels of cherub were found in newborn INPs, where it was cytoplasmic (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6A,B.

claim: Over time, cherub expression in INPs decreased and the lncRNA was only weakly detected in GMCs and neurons.
source: Over time, cherub expression in INPs decreased and the lncRNA was only weakly detected in GMCs and neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Adult brains showed no expression of cherub.
source: Consequently, adult brains showed no expression of cherub (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression pattern and the localization of cherub was conserved in other Drosophila species.
source: Notably, this expression pattern and the localization of cherub was conserved in other Drosophila species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The cortical pool of cherub localized asymmetrically in mitotic NBs, opposite to the apical marker aPKC.
source: Remarkably, the cortical pool of cherub localized asymmetrically in mitotic NBs, opposite to the apical marker aPKC and thus segregated into the INP upon cytokinesis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6C.

claim: 100% of mitotic NBIIs show cherub crescents.
source: 100% of mitotic NBIIs show cherub crescents (E) opposite to the apical aPKC crescent as measured by the angle between aPKC and cherub crescents.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6D,E showing in vitro analysis.

claim: All three cherub isoforms showed the same localization pattern and were asymmetrically segregated in NBIIs during mitosis.
source: However, the combination of FISH probes against specifically RC and regions present in RA and RC or RB and RC confirmed that all isoforms showed the same localization pattern and were asymmetrically segregated in NBIIs during mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–K).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–K.

claim: Expressing a constitutively active form of Lgl (Lgl3A) led to a uniformly cortical distribution of cherub.
source: While expressing a constitutively active form of Lgl (Lgl3A) led to a uniform cortical localization of cherub, the overexpression of a constitutively active form of aPKC (aPKC∆N) resulted in cytoplasmic cherub (Figure 6F).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The overexpression of a constitutively active form of aPKC (aPKC∆N) resulted in cytoplasmic cherub.
source: While expressing a constitutively active form of Lgl (Lgl3A) led to a uniform cortical localization of cherub, the overexpression of a constitutively active form of aPKC (aPKC∆N) resulted in cytoplasmic cherub (Figure 6F).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6F.

claim: Upon aPKC∆N expression, cherub levels are similar in NBIIs and their recently born daughter cell.
source: Upon the expression of aPKCΔN (n = 11 NB-daughter cell pairs from four different brains) or miranda RNAi (n = 12 NB-daughter cell pairs from four different brains), cherub levels are similar in NBIIs and their recently born (closest) daughter cell.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6G.

claim: Basal cherub polarity depended on Miranda.
source: Basal cherub polarity depended on Miranda (Figure 6F,G), a known adaptor protein required to tether proteins to the basal part of a NB's plasma membrane.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6F,G.

claim: Staufen has been described to enrich at the basal cell pole of dividing embryonic and larval NBs.
source: The Miranda-associated RNA-binding protein Staufen (Matsuzaki et al., 1998; Schuldt et al., 1998; Shen et al., 1998; Slack et al., 2007) has been described to enrich at the basal cell pole of dividing embryonic and larval NBs (Broadus et al., 1998; Jia et al., 2015; Li et al., 1997) and indeed it also localized asymmetrically in dividing NBIIs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Staufen was enriched in the most recently born iINPs and declined upon INP differentiation.
source: Consequently, Staufen was enriched in the most recently born iINPs and declined upon INP differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In staufen depleted NBIIs, cherub was no longer cortical, failed to segregate asymmetrically and accumulated in the cytoplasm.
source: In staufen depleted NBIIs, cherub was no longer cortical, failed to segregate asymmetrically and accumulated in the cytoplasm (Figure 6H,I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6H,I and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: qPCR on RNA isolated from anti-Staufen immunoprecipitates detected cherub but not the highly expressed control RNA RpL32.
source: qPCR on RNA, isolated from anti-Staufen immunoprecipitates, detected cherub but not the highly expressed control RNA RpL32 (Figure 6J).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6J showing RIP-qPCR results.

claim: In-silico analysis of cherub transcripts showed limited sequence similarity across Drosophila species.
source: In-silico analysis of cherub transcripts showed limited sequence similarity across Drosophila species (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B), but revealed four thermodynamically stable and evolutionary conserved secondary RNA structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: In-silico analysis revealed four thermodynamically stable and evolutionary conserved secondary RNA structures in cherub.
source: In-silico analysis of cherub transcripts showed limited sequence similarity across Drosophila species (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B), but revealed four thermodynamically stable and evolutionary conserved secondary RNA structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,C.

claim: The identified structures resemble stem loops previously described for Staufen binding.
source: The identified structures resemble stem loops previously described for Staufen binding (Ferrandon et al., 1994; Laver et al., 2013) and hence may constitute potential binding sites.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ferrandon et al., 1994; Laver et al., 2013.

claim: Binding to Staufen is required for segregating cherub into INPs to prevent its accumulation in NBIIs over time.
source: Therefore, binding to Staufen is required for segregating cherub into INPs to prevent its accumulation in NBIIs over time (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Staufen experiments and is illustrated in Figure 6K.

claim: Intensity measurements of nuclear cherub dots did not reveal any significant increase in brat RNAi tNBs.
source: Intensity measurements of nuclear cherub dots, which represent transcribed RNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), did not reveal any significant increase in brat RNAi tNBs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 7A.

claim: High cherub levels in brat tNBs are not due to transcriptional upregulation.
source: This suggests that high levels are not due to transcriptional upregulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the intensity measurements.

claim: Cortical cherub was strongly enhanced in brat tNBs.
source: Cortical cherub, in contrast, was strongly enhanced in brat tNBs (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and still asymmetrically inherited by one daughter cell in the majority of tNBs (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Temporal identity in NBIIs is controlled by opposing gradients of the RNA-binding proteins Imp and Syp.

claim: The transition from early Imp-positive to a late Syp-positive NB state is triggered by the nuclear receptor Seven-up (Svp).

claim: brat tumors depleted of cherub still expressed Syp, however Syp was no longer enriched at the cell cortex.

claim: brat mutant tNBs fail to fully progress to the late stages of temporal identity in a cherub-dependent manner.

claim: Imp depletion by RNAi significantly reduced tumor growth and increased the median survival time of tumor-bearing flies.
source: Advancing tNBs' temporal identity by svp overexpression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C) or Imp depletion by RNAi (Figure 8E,G,I) significantly reduced tumor growth and increased the median survival time (50% survival rate) of tumor-bearing flies.
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 8E,G,I.

claim: Shifting temporal identity of brat RNAi tNBs towards younger stages by svp misexpression significantly decreased the median survival rates.

claim: Syp RNAi significantly decreased the median survival rates indicating faster tumor growth.
source: Conversely, shifting temporal identity of brat RNAi tNBs towards younger stages by svp misexpression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) or Syp RNAi (Figure 8 - F, H, J) significantly decreased the median survival rates indicating faster tumor growth.

claim: Temporal identity defects are involved in brain tumor growth.
source: Thus, temporal identity defects are involved in brain tumor growth.

claim: In NBIIs Syp was localized at the cortex and also detected in the cytoplasm.

claim: Syp segregated asymmetrically in mitosis.

claim: Syp became enriched in the cytoplasm of the most recently-born INPs.
source: Similar to Staufen and cherub, Syp segregated asymmetrically in mitosis (Figure 9A–C), and became enriched in the cytoplasm of the most recently-born INPs (Figure 9D,E).

claim: Syp colocalized with Staufen and cherub in mitotic NBIIs.

claim: Binding between Staufen and Syp was lost upon RNA digestion or cherub depletion.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrated that Staufen and Syp are in a complex and binding between the two proteins was lost upon RNA digestion or cherub depletion (Figure 9F,G).
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 9F,G.

claim: RIP-qPCR experiments confirmed that cherub was enriched upon HA-tagged Syp pull-down.

evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 9H.

claim: cherub functions as adapter between Syp and Staufen.
source: These data suggest that cherub functions as adapter between Syp and Staufen (Figure 9I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation and RIP experiments, illustrated in Figure 9I.

claim: brat tumors do not require additional genetic lesions for the transition to an immortal state.
source: Surprisingly, however, our data indicate that brat tumors do not require additional genetic lesions for the transition to an immortal state.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the genomic analysis.

claim: Genomic instability alone can induce tumors in Drosophila epithelial cells.
source: This is not a general feature of Drosophila tumors as genomic instability alone can induce tumors in Drosophila epithelial cells (Dekanty et al., 2012) and intestinal stem cells (Siudeja et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dekanty et al., 2012 and Siudeja et al., 2015.

claim: Defects in genome integrity do not contribute to primary tumor formation in NBs.
source: However, our results are supported by previous experiments demonstrating that defects in genome integrity do not contribute to primary tumor formation in NBs (Castellanos et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Castellanos et al., 2008.

claim: Tumors induced by loss of epigenetic regulators in Drosophila wing discs do not display genome instability.
source: Similarly, tumors induced by loss of epigenetic regulators in Drosophila wing discs do not display genome instability (Sievers et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sievers et al., 2014.

claim: Childhood brain tumors only harbor an extremely low mutation rate and very few recurrent DNA alterations.
source: Interestingly, epigenetic tumorigenesis was described before in humans, where childhood brain tumors only harbor an extremely low mutation rate and very few recurrent DNA alterations (Lee et al., 2012; Mack et al., 2014; Northcott et al., 2012; Parsons et al., 2011; Pugh et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2012; Sausen et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to human cancer studies.

claim: Comparable observations of low mutation rates have been made for leukemia.
source: Comparable observations have been made for leukemia (Quesada et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Quesada et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2011.

claim: cherub is the first lncRNA described to segregate asymmetrically during mitosis.
source: cherub is the first lncRNA described to segregate asymmetrically during mitosis.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Once cherub is allocated through binding to Staufen into the cytoplasm of INPs, its levels decrease over time.
source: Once cherub is allocated through binding to the RNA-binding protein Staufen into the cytoplasm of INPs, its levels decrease over time.
evidence: This describes the dynamics of cherub in INPs.

claim: The inability to segregate cherub into differentiating cells leads to its accumulation in tNBs.
source: Our results show that the inability to segregate cherub into differentiating cells leads to its accumulation in tNBs.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: A vast number of lncRNAs show increased expression levels in various tumor types.
source: The increasing amount of tumor transcriptome data indicates that a vast number of lncRNAs show increased expression levels in various tumor types (Huarte, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Huarte, 2015.

claim: The mammalian homologue of cherub's binding partner Staufen has been described to asymmetrically localize RNA in dividing neural stem cells.
source: Intriguingly, the mammalian homologue of cherub's binding partner Staufen has been also described to asymmetrically localize RNA in dividing neural stem cells (Kusek et al., 2012; Vessey et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kusek et al., 2012; Vessey et al., 2012.

claim: tNBs retain the early temporal identity factor Imp even during late larval stages.
source: We show that tNBs retain the early temporal identity factor Imp even during late larval stages.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Imp expression in brat mutants is heterogeneous and only a subpopulation of tNBs maintains young identity.
source: However, Imp expression in brat mutants is heterogeneous and only a subpopulation of tNBs maintains young identity.
evidence: This describes the heterogeneity of temporal identity in tumors.

source: Tumor heterogeneity has also been described for pros tumors, where only a subset of tNBs maintains expression of the early temporal factors Imp and Chinmo (Narbonne-Reveau et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Narbonne-Reveau et al., 2016.

claim: In prospero tumors, the subpopulation that maintains early temporal factors drives tumor growth.
source: Interestingly, it is this subpopulation that drives tumor growth in prospero tumors.
evidence: This statement refers to findings in prospero tumors.

claim: 'Rejuvenating' tNBs enhances tumor growth and increases the survival of tumor bearing flies.
source: Consistent with this, our genetic experiments show that 'rejuvenating' tNBs enhances tumor growth and consequently increases the survival of tumor bearing flies, whereas 'aging' tNBs identity has the opposite effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genetic manipulation experiments.

source: Consistent with this, our genetic experiments show that 'rejuvenating' tNBs enhances tumor growth and consequently increases the survival of tumor bearing flies, whereas 'aging' tNBs identity has the opposite effect.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the genetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Upregulated expression of mammalian counterparts of Imp has been implied in various cancer types.
source: Although mammalian counterparts of Imp have not yet being shown to act as temporal identity genes, their upregulated expression has been implied in various cancer types (Dai et al., 2017; Lederer et al., 2014).

claim: Temporal patterning of NBs has an essential role in brain tumor propagation in Drosophila.
source: Therefore, temporal patterning of NBs has an essential role in brain tumor propagation in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the temporal identity experiments.

evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: cherub regulates Syp localization by facilitating the binding of Syp to Staufen and thus recruiting it to the cell cortex.
source: In NBs and tNBs cherub regulates Syp localization by facilitating the binding of Syp to Staufen and thus recruiting it to the cell cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: In tumors depleted of cherub, Syp localizes mainly to the cytoplasm and is no longer observed at the cortex.
source: In tumors depleted of cherub, Syp localizes mainly to the cytoplasm and is no longer observed at the cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The removal of Syp in tNBs leads to enhanced tumor growth and early lethality.
source: As the removal of Syp in tNBs leads to enhanced tumor growth and early lethality, those data suggest that cherub could control temporal NB identity by regulating the subcellular localization of Syp.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The RNA-binding protein Syp is a translational regulator.
source: The RNA-binding protein Syp is a translational regulator (Duning et al., 2008; McDermott et al., 2012; 2014) and has been suggested to control mRNA stability (Yang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duning et al., 2008; McDermott et al., 2012; 2014; Yang et al., 2017b.

claim: Mammalian SYNCRIP/hnRNP Q interacts with a lncRNA that suppresses translation.
source: As mammalian SYNCRIP/hnRNP Q interacts with a lncRNA that suppresses translation (Duning et al., 2008; Kondrashov et al., 2005), cherub might regulate Syp to inhibit or promote the translation of a subset of target mRNAs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duning et al., 2008; Kondrashov et al., 2005.

claim: In NBs Syp acts at two stages during development: repressing early temporal NB factors approximately 60 hr after larval hatching, and promoting levels of prospero at the end of the NB lifespan.
source: In particular, in NBs Syp acts at two stages in NBs during development: Firstly, approximately 60 hr after larval hatching it represses early temporal NB factors, like Imp (Syed et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017a). Secondly, at the end of the NB lifespan Syp promotes levels of the differentiation factor prospero to facilitate the NB's final cell cycle exit (Yang et al., 2017a; Yang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Syed et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017a; Yang et al., 2017b.

claim: cherub mutants are viable, fertile and do not affect NBII lineages.

evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: cherub mutants show normal geotaxis.
source: As cherub mutants show normal geotaxis, function of the lncRNA seems dispensable for NBIIs to generate their neural descendants.

source: There are several possibilities why we do not observe a phenotype upon the loss of cherub. In wild-type flies cherub might confer robustness. A similar scenario was observed in embryonic NBs, in which Staufen segregates prospero mRNA into GMCs (Broadus et al., 1998; Schuldt et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Broadus et al., 1998; Schuldt et al., 1998.

claim: The failure to segregate prospero mRNA does not result in a phenotype, but it enhances the hypomorphic prospero GMC phenotype.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Broadus et al., 1998.
